10004717.p001.s001.text: MdWRKY120 Enhance Apple Susceptibility to Alternaria alternata

10004717.p002.s001.text: Alternaria alternata (A. alternata) is a common pathogen that greatly influences apples’ quantity and quality.

10004717.p002.s002.text: However, chemical treatments produce increased health risks along with decreased food and environmental safety.

10004717.p002.s003.text: Advancements in plant molecular biology, such as transgenic technology, have increased apple trees’ resistance to pathogens and have therefore attracted widespread attention.

10004717.p002.s004.text: WRKY transcription factors are involved in abiotic and biotic stress regulation; however, their biological role in non-model plants such as apple, is still unknown.

10004717.p002.s005.text: In this investigation, MdWRKY120 was isolated from the ‘GL-3′ apple to determine its function during Alternaria alternate infection.

10004717.p002.s006.text: The MdWRKY120-GFP fusion protein was located in the nucleus.

10004717.p002.s007.text: MdWRKY120 in yeast cells exhibited activating transcriptional activity, meaning it is a transcription activator.

10004717.p002.s008.text: MdWRKY120 overexpression transgenic plants were more sensitive to A. alternata, while RNAi transgenic plants showed increased resistance to A. alternata.

10004717.p002.s009.text: This investigation demonstrates that MdWRKY120 enhances the susceptibility of apples to A. alternata.

10004717.p005.s001.text: The WRKY family is an important transcription factor family in higher plants, regulating growth and development.

10004717.p005.s002.text: The WRKY transcription factor contains at least 1~60 amino acids-long conserved domain of WRKY, a highly conserved N-terminal heptapeptide called WRKYGQK, and a C-terminal-, C2H2-, or C2HC-type zinc finger structure.

10004717.p005.s003.text: Based on the number of WRKY conserved domains and the type of zinc finger structure, the WRKY transcription factors are classified into three groups.

10004717.p005.s004.text: Genome sequencing has helped identify many WRKY gene families in various crops.

10004717.p005.s005.text: Arabidopsis thaliana consists of 75 genes, the apple of 127 genes, maize of 119 genes, and rice of 103 genes.

10004717.p005.s006.text: The WRKY family is crucial for regulating biotic and abiotic stress, such as drought, salt stress, disease resistance, seed germination, and flower development.

10004717.p006.s001.text: As has been recently reported, WRKY40s are essential for plant immune response.

10004717.p006.s002.text: WRKY protein’s function against biotic stresses in horticultural plant species has also been studied.

10004717.p006.s003.text: In pepper immunity, WRKY40 directly regulates ChiIV3 expression level, thereby significantly increasing its resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum.

10004717.p006.s004.text: It was also found that, in the resistant (WR315) plants, there was WRKY40 up-regulation under Fusarium stress, whereas, in susceptible (JG62) plants, it lacked expression.

10004717.p006.s005.text: Furthermore, in Arabidopsis, heterologous chickpea WRKY40 over-expression stimulated an immune response against Pseudomonas syringae.

10004717.p006.s006.text: In Arabidopsis, simultaneous WRKY18 and WRKY40 mutations render otherwise susceptible wild-type species resistant to the Golovinomyces orontii, a biotrophic powdery mildew fungus.

10004717.p006.s007.text: In some species, WRKY40 is reported to have opposite regulations; for instance, the GhWRKY40 transcription levels in cotton increased after bacterial pathogen R. solanacearum infection, and it improved most of the defense-associated genes, increased the wounding tolerance, and the resisitance to R. solanacearum.

10004717.p006.s008.text: Overall, WRKY40 significantly regulates a variety of plant stress responses; however, little is known about its function in apples against A. alternata.

10004717.p007.s001.text: In our previous study, we found that AtWRKY40 and MdWRKY120 are homologous genes and, thus, it was hypothesized that they have similar functions.

10004717.p007.s002.text: Therefore, this study is focused on MdWRKY120, which was expressed in all the studied tissues and was relatively high in the fruit and root.

10004717.p007.s003.text: The green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeled MdWRKY120 protein was localized in the nucleus and displayed transcriptional activity in yeast cells.

10004717.p007.s004.text: When non-transformed plants were compared with overly expressed MdWRKY120 plants, the latter were more susceptible to A. alternata.

10004717.p007.s005.text: Overall, MdWRKY120 is crucial for regulating A. alternata resistance in apples.

10004717.p007.s006.text: This study on MdWRKY120 against A. alternata resistance will pave the foundation for the molecular genetic breeding of apple disease resistance.

10004717.p010.s001.text: The apple’s transcription factor MdWRKY120 gene sequence was downloaded from the JGI database ( accessed on 2 November 2022).

10004717.p010.s002.text: To investigate the evolutionary association between MdWRKY120 and other WRKY proteins, a phylogenetic evaluation was carried out of MEGA 6.06 software by the Neighbor-Joining method.

10004717.p010.s003.text: As indicated by Figure 1a, MdWRKY120 is closely related to PbWRKY120 in pear.

10004717.p010.s004.text: The sequence alignment of MdWRKY120 amino acid and other WRKY120 proteins revealed one shared conversed WRKY domain (Figure 1b).

10004717.p010.s005.text: Since the WRKY120 transition factor is involved in pathogen defense and stress response, its close homology in various species may indicate some similar functions, especially in A. alternate defense, and some of these proteins are reported to take part in plantss defense against bacteria and fungi.

10004717.p012.s001.text: For elucidating MdWRKY120 expression levels in various tissues, real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed using four-year-old ‘GL-3’ trees.

10004717.p012.s002.text: The results indicated that MdWRKY120 was expressed in different tissues, including flower, stem, leaf, root, and fruit, with the highest levels in the fruit (Figure 2).

10004717.p013.s001.text: To determine the mechanism responsible for MdWRKY120′s expression patterns, its promoter region of 1591 bp was evaluated.

10004717.p013.s002.text: The Plant CARE database predicted various response elements for biotic and abiotic stresses, such as hormone responses, tissue-specific expression, light, and development, as shown in Table S2.

10004717.p013.s004.text: The data collected from the above experiments suggested that MdWRKY120 may be involved in defense and stress.

10004717.p015.s001.text: It was reported that most WRKYs were nucleus-localized proteins.

10004717.p015.s002.text: To elucidate whether MdWRKY120 was a nuclear protein like other WRKYs, the MdWRKY120 coding sequence was attached to the pRI-GFP via the CaMV 35S promoter, followed by transient expression of the MdWRKY120-GFP fusion gene in tobacco leaves.

10004717.p015.s003.text: As indicated by Figure 3, the MdWRKY120-GFP fusion protein’s signals were limited to the nucleus, whereas the positive control GFP signals were expressed throughout the cell, proving that MdWRKY120 was localized in the nucleus and is thus a nuclear protein.

10004717.p017.s001.text: To analyze the transcriptional activity of MdWRKY120, the complete MdWRKY120 coding sequence was inserted into pGBT9 to obtain the pGBT9-MdWRKY120 construct, which was then transformed in the yeast cells.

10004717.p017.s002.text: The empty pGBT9 vector was kept as the negative control.

10004717.p017.s003.text: As Figure 4 indicates, the Y2H Gold yeast strain containing pGBT9 only propagated in SD/-Trp, while the yeast strain containing pGBT9-MdWRKY120 propagated in both SD/-Trp and SD/-Trp-His-Ade with X-α-Gal.

10004717.p017.s004.text: The result indicated that MdWRKY120 was a transcription activator.

10004717.p018.s001.text: 2.5. Overexpression and RNAi Knockdown of MdWRKY120 in ‘GL-3′ Apple

10004717.p019.s001.text: Furthermore, to investigate the extent to which its role is important, especially MdWRKY120’s response to A. alternata in apples, overly expressed ‘GL-3′ apples were developed by transforming with the pRI101-MdWRKY120 plasmid.

10004717.p019.s002.text: Putative transgenic plants were acquired via Agrobacterium-mediated ‘GL-3′ apples’ transformation, performed following the instructions of Zhang et al.. Six independent kanamycin-resistant MdWRKY120-overexpressing apple plants were propagated; its overexpression was subsequently determined by PCR analysis using a primer set MdWRKY120F/MdWRKY120R.

10004717.p019.s003.text: A 963 bp band from the genomic DNA of 3 overly-expressed MdWRKY120 transgenic lines was amplified.

10004717.p019.s004.text: No corresponding bands were observed in ‘GL-3′ plants (Figure 5b).

10004717.p019.s005.text: Compared with non-transformed control plants, the MdWRKY120 expressions in the 3 lines were notably enhanced.

10004717.p019.s006.text: The relative MdWRKY120 expressions were remarkably enhanced in OE1, and OE1 -4 and -5 (Figure 5c).

10004717.p019.s007.text: Thus, the MdWRKY120 was successfully overexpressed in apples with high levels and OE1 and OE5 were selected for further investigation.

10004717.p019.s008.text: ‘GL-3′ apples’ MdWRKY120 RNAi silencing was also carried out via Agrobacterium-mediated transformation.

10004717.p019.s009.text: Three independent kanamycin-resistant plants were propagated and authenticated by PCR (Figure 5e) and qRT-PCR (Figure 5f).

10004717.p019.s010.text: The MdWRKY120 expression in these propagated plants was sharply decreased, and RNAi-2 and RNAi-5 were chosen to represent MdWRKY120-RNAi transgenic plants.

PMC10004717.p001.text: MdWRKY120 Enhance Apple Susceptibility to Alternaria alternata

PMC10004717.p002.text: Alternaria alternata (A. alternata) is a common pathogen that greatly influences apples’ quantity and quality. However, chemical treatments produce increased health risks along with decreased food and environmental safety. Advancements in plant molecular biology, such as transgenic technology, have increased apple trees’ resistance to pathogens and have therefore attracted widespread attention. WRKY transcription factors are involved in abiotic and biotic stress regulation; however, their biological role in non-model plants such as apple, is still unknown. In this investigation, MdWRKY120 was isolated from the ‘GL-3′ apple to determine its function during Alternaria alternate infection. The MdWRKY120-GFP fusion protein was located in the nucleus. MdWRKY120 in yeast cells exhibited activating transcriptional activity, meaning it is a transcription activator. MdWRKY120 overexpression transgenic plants were more sensitive to A. alternata, while RNAi transgenic plants showed increased resistance to A. alternata. This investigation demonstrates that MdWRKY120 enhances the susceptibility of apples to A. alternata.

PMC10004717.p005.text: The WRKY family is an important transcription factor family in higher plants, regulating growth and development. The WRKY transcription factor contains at least 1~60 amino acids-long conserved domain of WRKY, a highly conserved N-terminal heptapeptide called WRKYGQK, and a C-terminal-, C2H2-, or C2HC-type zinc finger structure. Based on the number of WRKY conserved domains and the type of zinc finger structure, the WRKY transcription factors are classified into three groups. Genome sequencing has helped identify many WRKY gene families in various crops. Arabidopsis thaliana consists of 75 genes, the apple of 127 genes, maize of 119 genes, and rice of 103 genes. The WRKY family is crucial for regulating biotic and abiotic stress, such as drought, salt stress, disease resistance, seed germination, and flower development.

PMC10004717.p006.text: As has been recently reported, WRKY40s are essential for plant immune response. WRKY protein’s function against biotic stresses in horticultural plant species has also been studied. In pepper immunity, WRKY40 directly regulates ChiIV3 expression level, thereby significantly increasing its resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum. It was also found that, in the resistant (WR315) plants, there was WRKY40 up-regulation under Fusarium stress, whereas, in susceptible (JG62) plants, it lacked expression. Furthermore, in Arabidopsis, heterologous chickpea WRKY40 over-expression stimulated an immune response against Pseudomonas syringae. In Arabidopsis, simultaneous WRKY18 and WRKY40 mutations render otherwise susceptible wild-type species resistant to the Golovinomyces orontii, a biotrophic powdery mildew fungus. In some species, WRKY40 is reported to have opposite regulations; for instance, the GhWRKY40 transcription levels in cotton increased after bacterial pathogen R. solanacearum infection, and it improved most of the defense-associated genes, increased the wounding tolerance, and the resisitance to R. solanacearum. Overall, WRKY40 significantly regulates a variety of plant stress responses; however, little is known about its function in apples against A. alternata.

PMC10004717.p007.text: In our previous study, we found that AtWRKY40 and MdWRKY120 are homologous genes and, thus, it was hypothesized that they have similar functions. Therefore, this study is focused on MdWRKY120, which was expressed in all the studied tissues and was relatively high in the fruit and root. The green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeled MdWRKY120 protein was localized in the nucleus and displayed transcriptional activity in yeast cells. When non-transformed plants were compared with overly expressed MdWRKY120 plants, the latter were more susceptible to A. alternata. Overall, MdWRKY120 is crucial for regulating A. alternata resistance in apples. This study on MdWRKY120 against A. alternata resistance will pave the foundation for the molecular genetic breeding of apple disease resistance.

PMC10004717.p010.text: The apple’s transcription factor MdWRKY120 gene sequence was downloaded from the JGI database ( accessed on 2 November 2022). To investigate the evolutionary association between MdWRKY120 and other WRKY proteins, a phylogenetic evaluation was carried out of MEGA 6.06 software by the Neighbor-Joining method. As indicated by Figure 1a, MdWRKY120 is closely related to PbWRKY120 in pear. The sequence alignment of MdWRKY120 amino acid and other WRKY120 proteins revealed one shared conversed WRKY domain (Figure 1b). Since the WRKY120 transition factor is involved in pathogen defense and stress response, its close homology in various species may indicate some similar functions, especially in A. alternate defense, and some of these proteins are reported to take part in plantss defense against bacteria and fungi.

PMC10004717.p012.text: For elucidating MdWRKY120 expression levels in various tissues, real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed using four-year-old ‘GL-3’ trees. The results indicated that MdWRKY120 was expressed in different tissues, including flower, stem, leaf, root, and fruit, with the highest levels in the fruit (Figure 2).

PMC10004717.p013.text: To determine the mechanism responsible for MdWRKY120′s expression patterns, its promoter region of 1591 bp was evaluated. The Plant CARE database predicted various response elements for biotic and abiotic stresses, such as hormone responses, tissue-specific expression, light, and development, as shown in Table S2. The core W-box, GARE cis-acting elements were found in the MdWRKY120 promoter region. The data collected from the above experiments suggested that MdWRKY120 may be involved in defense and stress.

PMC10004717.p015.text: It was reported that most WRKYs were nucleus-localized proteins. To elucidate whether MdWRKY120 was a nuclear protein like other WRKYs, the MdWRKY120 coding sequence was attached to the pRI-GFP via the CaMV 35S promoter, followed by transient expression of the MdWRKY120-GFP fusion gene in tobacco leaves. As indicated by Figure 3, the MdWRKY120-GFP fusion protein’s signals were limited to the nucleus, whereas the positive control GFP signals were expressed throughout the cell, proving that MdWRKY120 was localized in the nucleus and is thus a nuclear protein.

PMC10004717.p017.text: To analyze the transcriptional activity of MdWRKY120, the complete MdWRKY120 coding sequence was inserted into pGBT9 to obtain the pGBT9-MdWRKY120 construct, which was then transformed in the yeast cells. The empty pGBT9 vector was kept as the negative control. As Figure 4 indicates, the Y2H Gold yeast strain containing pGBT9 only propagated in SD/-Trp, while the yeast strain containing pGBT9-MdWRKY120 propagated in both SD/-Trp and SD/-Trp-His-Ade with X-α-Gal. The result indicated that MdWRKY120 was a transcription activator.

PMC10004717.p018.text: 2.5. Overexpression and RNAi Knockdown of MdWRKY120 in ‘GL-3′ Apple

PMC10004717.p019.text: Furthermore, to investigate the extent to which its role is important, especially MdWRKY120’s response to A. alternata in apples, overly expressed ‘GL-3′ apples were developed by transforming with the pRI101-MdWRKY120 plasmid. Putative transgenic plants were acquired via Agrobacterium-mediated ‘GL-3′ apples’ transformation, performed following the instructions of Zhang et al.. Six independent kanamycin-resistant MdWRKY120-overexpressing apple plants were propagated; its overexpression was subsequently determined by PCR analysis using a primer set MdWRKY120F/MdWRKY120R. A 963 bp band from the genomic DNA of 3 overly-expressed MdWRKY120 transgenic lines was amplified. No corresponding bands were observed in ‘GL-3′ plants (Figure 5b). Compared with non-transformed control plants, the MdWRKY120 expressions in the 3 lines were notably enhanced. The relative MdWRKY120 expressions were remarkably enhanced in OE1, and OE1 -4 and -5 (Figure 5c). Thus, the MdWRKY120 was successfully overexpressed in apples with high levels and OE1 and OE5 were selected for further investigation. ‘GL-3′ apples’ MdWRKY120 RNAi silencing was also carried out via Agrobacterium-mediated transformation. Three independent kanamycin-resistant plants were propagated and authenticated by PCR (Figure 5e) and qRT-PCR (Figure 5f). The MdWRKY120 expression in these propagated plants was sharply decreased, and RNAi-2 and RNAi-5 were chosen to represent MdWRKY120-RNAi transgenic plants.

PMC10004717.p020.text: 2.6. MdWRKY120 Confers A. Alternata Resistance to Apple

PMC10004717.p021.text: In A. alternate-infected apples, there was subsequent cell death. The circular black or brownish spots on the leaves expanded in late spring to early summer, eventually causing defoliation. To figure out the role of MdWRKY120 in defending against A. alternata, the leaves 5 days post fungi inoculation were observed and the morbidity and disease index was analyzed. As shown in Figure 6a, after 2 days of fungi inoculation, brown spots appeared in MdWRKY120-RNAi plants and controls, while brown spots were much more obvious in overexpressed plants. After 3 days of inoculation, the overexpressed plants showed more disease spots than MdWRKY120-RNAi plants. In gene-silenced plants, no disease spots appeared until 5 days after inoculation. Moreover, the area of disease spots in MdWRKY120-silenced plants was markedly smaller than that in overexpression and control plants. In brief, after 5 days of inoculation, the morbidity in MdWRKY120-RNAi plants was <45%, compared with >80% morbidity of MdWRKY120 overexpressed plants and 65% of control plants (Figure 6b). The statistics of disease index after 4 days of inoculation in overexpressed plants was lower and, in the gene-silenced plants, was higher than the control. The result indicated that MdWRKY120 enhances apple susceptibility to spotted leaf litter pathogen.

PMC10004717.p024.text: The literature suggests the involvement of WRKY proteins in microbe-associated molecular pattern-triggered immunity and other important mechanisms. The immune system of plants has two models, including (1) PAMP-triggered immunity, and (2) effector-triggered immunity. Pathogen resistance is a complicated process involving transcriptional regulation, and transcription factors are essential for plant defense responses. With the recent rapid advancements in molecular biology and transgenic technology, plants’ immunity can be improved by genetic modification. WRKY transcription factors directly or indirectly regulate the expression of downstream stress resistance genes (such as disease resistance-related genes, PR) and improve pathogenic resistance by regulating the immune response in many species. In a preliminary study, Hawthorns infected by apple chlorotic leaf spot virus (ACLSV) were investigated by high-throughput sequencing, and it was found that plant-pathogen interaction-related genes (WRKY transcription factors) were significantly up-regulated in the infected group.

PMC10004717.p025.text: WRKY40 (WRKY family member) is associated with resistance against biotic stress. Many complex and overlapping networks, including WRKYs, regulate multiple biological processes in plants. The heterologous expression of GhWRKY40 enhanced the susceptibility of tobacco to R. solanacearum and its reduction in the expression of PR1 and PR2 genes in the SA signal transduction pathway, ACS6 genes in the ET signal transduction pathway, and JAZ1 and JAZ3 genes in the JA signal transduction pathway has been reported. In poplar plants, PtrWRKY40 overexpression enhances its sensitivity to ulcerative pathogens and decreases the expression of genes related to SA signaling pathways PR1.1, PR2.1, PR5.9, and CPR5. These results suggest that WRKY40 proteins are the transcription factors that are functionally conserved and regulate plants’ abiotic stress response. According to phylogenetic alignment, MdWRKY120 and AtWRKY40 are homologous genes. MdWRKY120 protein had activating transcriptional activity and its overexpression reduced the resistance to A. alternata. Unlike other species, WRKY40 family genes play a negative regulatory role in the immune resistance mechanism against spotted fall disease in apples. An in-depth investigation to evaluate the exact mechanism is needed. This research puts forth crucial information regarding the apple plants’ resistance to Alternaria.
